prompt: In this lesson, `google-genai` and `cohere` send every request to labembed. What is labembed?
hint: Read what it refuses.

choices.text: A course-written server running two local models
choices.why: Right. The SDKs are real and unmodified, and the vectors are real, from all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and WordLlama; the models are not Google's or Cohere's.

choices.text: Google's gemini-embedding-001, downloaded and run locally
choices.why: labembed refuses the name gemini-embedding-001 with a 404. It serves only lab-minilm and lab-wordllama.

choices.text: A proxy that forwards each request to Google or Cohere and logs it
choices.why: No request left the machine. The providers' APIs were unreachable, which is why the stand-in exists.

choices.text: A mock that returns random numbers of the right length
choices.why: The vectors are computed by two real models for every request, which is why the searches in this lesson find the right articles.

prompt: You call `embed_content` with a list of three titles. How do you tell which returned embedding belongs to which title?
hint: Compare with the OpenAI response from lesson 7.

choices.text: Each embedding carries an `index` field naming its input
choices.why: That is OpenAI's response. Gemini's embeddings carry `values` and nothing that points back to the input.

choices.text: By position: `r.embeddings` is in the order the titles were sent
choices.why: Yes. The order is the only link, so keep the list you sent beside the response.

choices.text: Each embedding repeats the text it was made from
choices.why: Neither the SDK object nor the JSON carries the text back; only the numbers return.

choices.text: Sort the embeddings by their first value to restore the order
choices.why: A coordinate on its own means nothing (lesson 1), and sorting by it would scramble the order rather than recover it.

prompt: A colleague moves from labembed to Google, asks gemini-embedding-001 for `output_dimensionality=768`, and ranks articles by the raw dot product of the returned values. What goes wrong?
hint: In the lab the lengths printed 1.0. Who made them 1.0?

choices.text: Nothing: the dot product of any two embeddings is already a cosine
choices.why: Only for unit vectors. labembed renormalises after truncating; Google documents that it does not for sizes below 3,072.

choices.text: The request fails, since the model accepts only its full 3,072
choices.why: 768 is one of the sizes Google recommends for this model, and the request succeeds.

choices.text: The vectors are not unit length, so the dot product is not a cosine
choices.why: Right. A truncated unit vector is shorter than 1, by a different amount for each text, so the dot product stops being a cosine. The last part of gemini.py is the fix.

choices.text: A dot product must be replaced by Hamming distance for truncated vectors
choices.why: Hamming distance compares bits. These are still float vectors; they only need normalising.

prompt: Google documents that only gemini-embedding-001's full 3,072-number output comes back ___, so a shorter one must be divided by its own length.
hint: It is what makes a dot product a cosine.

prompt: Why does a model trained for asymmetric search embed a query differently from a document?
hint: Compare *can I pay in three parts* with *Payment methods we accept*.

choices.text: Queries are embedded with fewer numbers to keep searches cheap
choices.why: Both sides come out at the same dimension, or they could not be compared at all.

choices.text: A question and the passage answering it are different texts
choices.why: Yes. Trained on question and answer pairs with the side marked, it puts a question near its answers rather than near similar questions.

choices.text: Documents are usually in another language from the queries
choices.why: Language has nothing to do with it. The help centre's questions and articles are both English and still differ in role.

choices.text: Documents are longer than the model's input limit and have to be cut
choices.why: The input limit applies to every text whatever its type; the type says what the text is for, not how long it is.

prompt: `tasks.py` embedded one question as `RETRIEVAL_QUERY`, `RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT`, `SEMANTIC_SIMILARITY` and `CLASSIFICATION`, and every difference printed 0.0. What does that show?
hint: The log shows what the server received.

choices.text: Task types change nothing for any model, Google's included
choices.why: Only labembed was measured. gemini-embedding-001 is documented to embed the types differently, and no request reached it.

choices.text: The SDK dropped the task type before sending the request
choices.why: The log recorded four different task types arriving, so the SDK sent them.

choices.text: labembed's models are symmetric, so the type changes nothing
choices.why: Right. Neither lab model has a query side and a document side, so there is no second way to embed the text.

choices.text: The server cached the vector from the first call and returned it three more times
choices.why: labembed computes every request; the vectors are identical because the model has only one way to embed a text.

prompt: Put the steps of a help-centre search with Gemini task types in order, from building the index to answering a customer.
hint: Indexing happens before anybody asks.
items: Store the vectors with the model and task type beside them
Score the question's vector against the stored ones
trap: The question is not embedded before the articles are stored: the index is built once, ahead of time, and each question is embedded when it arrives.

prompt: A team indexes its articles with `SEMANTIC_SIMILARITY` and searches them with `RETRIEVAL_QUERY` against gemini-embedding-001. What happens?
hint: Ask what each call, on its own, looks like to the API.

choices.text: The second call fails with a 400, since the types do not match
choices.why: Each request names one valid type, and the API sees one request at a time. Nothing compares the two.

choices.text: Every call succeeds, and the mismatch goes unreported
choices.why: Yes. The mismatch lives between two calls, so only a measurement on the team's own questions would show it.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because every task type gives the same vector
choices.why: That is labembed, whose models are symmetric. Google's model is documented to embed the types differently.

choices.text: The search refuses to run until the index is rebuilt with a query type
choices.why: Nothing in the API knows how the index was built, and indexing with a query type would be the wrong fix anyway.

prompt: `co.embed(model="lab-minilm", texts=["Audiobooks"])` raised a `TypeError`. Where was the call refused?
hint: A TypeError is a Python exception about arguments.

choices.text: In labembed, which answered with a 400
choices.why: The 400 came from the hand-written curl request. The SDK call never reached the server.

choices.text: In Python, by the SDK, before any request was built
choices.why: Right. `input_type` is a required keyword argument of `embed`, so Python refused the call.

choices.text: At Cohere's servers, which reject requests from the lab
choices.why: No request went to Cohere; every request in this lesson went to labembed.

choices.text: In the operating system, because port 8500 was closed
choices.why: The same script's next call reached the server and got a 400, so the port was open.

prompt: A job embeds 1,000 product descriptions through Cohere's endpoint with the slicing loop from `embed_all`, 96 texts per call. How many calls does it make?
hint: The last call takes whatever is left over.

prompt: A batch job against Cohere gets a 400 saying `too many texts: 120 (the limit is 96)`. What is the right fix?
hint: Will the same request ever succeed?

choices.text: Retry the same call after a short pause, as for a 429
choices.why: A 429 is about timing and passes; this 400 is about the request itself, and the same call fails every time.

choices.text: Switch `input_type` to `classification`, which accepts more texts
choices.why: The limit is per call, whatever the input type.

choices.text: Ask for `int8` instead of `float` so that more texts fit
choices.why: The limit counts texts in, not bytes out.

choices.text: Cut the list into slices of at most 96 and send one call per slice
choices.why: Yes. That is `embed_all`: the error is a bug in the slice size, and the fix is in the loop.

prompt: The cohere SDK puts the ordinary 32-bit vectors in `r.embeddings.___`, with a trailing underscore because the plain word is a Python built-in.
hint: The attribute is named after the encoding, plus one character.

prompt: Match each Cohere `input_type` to the text it is meant for.
hint: Two of them are the sides of a search.

pairs.right: An article stored so it can be found
What a customer types into the search box
A ticket that will be a classifier's input
One of many messages grouped with no labels

right_distractors: A vector reduced to one bit per coordinate

prompt: `search.py` found 19 at rank 1 and 22 in the top 3 with queries sent as `search_query`, `search_document` and `clustering` alike. What can you conclude?
hint: Which server answered, and what does it do with the type?

choices.text: Input types never matter, so production code can leave them out
choices.why: Cohere requires the parameter, and against an asymmetric model the wrong type is a silent loss. One symmetric model says nothing about the rest.

choices.text: Only that labembed ignores the type
choices.why: Right. labembed embeds a text the same way whatever the type, so the three runs compared identical vectors.

choices.text: `clustering` is as good as `search_query` for search with Cohere's models
choices.why: No Cohere model was measured. The run shows only what a symmetric model does.

choices.text: 24 questions are too few for any difference between types to show
choices.why: The vectors were identical, so no number of questions would have shown a difference here.

prompt: Marginalia trains lesson 4's logistic regression on Cohere vectors of 100 tickets embedded as `classification`. A new ticket arrives to be labelled. Which `input_type` should it be embedded with?
hint: Is classification a pair of sides, or one kind of text?

choices.text: `search_query`, because a new ticket is like a question asked of the training set
choices.why: Classification is not a search. The classifier reads features, and they have to be made the same way as the ones it was trained on.

choices.text: `search_document`, because the new ticket will be stored afterwards
choices.why: Storing it later does not change what this vector is for now: an input to the classifier.

choices.text: `classification`, like the rest
choices.why: Yes. Classification is symmetric: every ticket is the same kind of text, so the new one is embedded exactly like the training set.

choices.text: `clustering`, because the new ticket has no label yet
choices.why: Clustering is for grouping without any labels. Here a trained classifier with labels is waiting for a feature vector like the ones it learned from.

prompt: A lab-wordllama vector has 256 coordinates. How many bytes does its `ubinary` form take?
hint: One bit per coordinate, eight bits to a byte.

prompt: In `quantised.py`, MiniLM's binary vectors put 23 of the 24 queries in the top 3, against 22 for float. What is the right reading?
hint: How many queries is the difference?

choices.text: Binary vectors are more accurate than float ones for this model
choices.why: One query out of 24 moving is within chance; it does not show binary is better.

choices.text: The float run had a bug that the binary run avoided
choices.why: Both runs scored the same vectors in different encodings, and float gave the same 22 as `search.py`.

choices.text: One query in 24 moving is chance, and shows nothing more
choices.why: Right. The honest conclusion is that the binary form cost nothing this small measurement can see.

choices.text: Hamming distance is a better measure than the dot product for every model
choices.why: WordLlama's binary run fell from 20 to 15 at rank 1, so it is not better for every model.

prompt: Why does `quantised.py` convert int8 vectors to 32-bit integers before taking the dot product?
hint: What is the largest sum 384 products of numbers near 127 can reach?

choices.text: NumPy refuses to multiply two int8 arrays
choices.why: NumPy multiplies them happily, in int8, and that is the problem: the result wraps around silently.

choices.text: The sum of hundreds of products of numbers up to 127 does not fit in eight bits
choices.why: Yes. One product alone can reach 16,129; in int8 the sum would overflow and wrap without an error.

choices.text: Converting makes the result a cosine
choices.why: The int8 dot product is not a cosine in any type; it only has to rank in the same order.

choices.text: Cohere returns int8 vectors as 32-bit integers anyway
choices.why: They arrive as lists of small whole numbers, and the program stores them as int8 on purpose.

prompt: Binary encoding took WordLlama from 20 to 15 at rank 1 and MiniLM from 19 to 16. Which explanation fits what the lesson measured?
hint: Count the bits each binary vector has.

choices.text: WordLlama is a static model, and static models cannot be binarised
choices.why: Its binary vectors were made and searched; they found 15 at rank 1. The loss is a matter of degree.

choices.text: labembed's int8 scaling damaged WordLlama's vectors before they were binarised
choices.why: The binary form is made from the signs of the float vector, not from the int8 one, and WordLlama's int8 run lost nothing at rank 1.

choices.text: WordLlama's float vectors are not unit length, so its bits are wrong
choices.why: labembed normalises every lab-wordllama vector, and the sign of a coordinate does not depend on the length anyway.

choices.text: Its 256 coordinates leave fewer bits to separate close articles than 384 do
choices.why: Right. One bit per coordinate keeps only a sign, and with fewer coordinates more articles land at nearly the same distance.

prompt: At the sheet's price for gemini-embedding-001, how many dollars does embedding 40 million tokens cost?
hint: The price is per million tokens.

prompt: Where do the prices in this lesson come from?
hint: The prices are pinned to something.

choices.text: The providers' own pricing pages, fetched on the day of recording
choices.why: Those pages could not be reached from the recording machine; the lesson says so.

choices.text: labembed's `billed_units`, multiplied by a rate the lab sets
choices.why: `billed_units` counts the lab's own tokens and carries no price at all.

choices.text: A third party's sheet, pinned to one commit
choices.why: Right. Pinning commit b9e71e990aed makes the sheet read the same next year, even if the providers' prices change.

choices.text: Token counts from tiktoken, times OpenAI's published rate for every provider
choices.why: Each provider has its own row and its own price on the sheet; tiktoken counts tokens and knows no prices.

prompt: An article runs to 3,000 tokens and you want it embedded whole, as one input. Which model on the sheet reads that much?
hint: Read the `max in` column.

choices.text: gemini-embedding-001
choices.why: It reads 2,048 tokens, so the end of a 3,000-token article would not be in the vector.

choices.text: embed-english-v3.0
choices.why: The sheet gives it 512 tokens, far below 3,000.

choices.text: text-embedding-3-small
choices.why: Yes. The sheet gives it 8,191 input tokens, enough for the article in one piece.

choices.text: embed-multilingual-v3.0
choices.why: Like the English v3 model, it reads 512 tokens.

prompt: Match each parameter to what it does and whose API it belongs to.
hint: Two of them belong to Google.

pairs.right: OpenAI: return fewer numbers per vector
Google: return fewer numbers per vector
Google: say what the text is for, optionally
Cohere: say what the text is for, required

right_distractors: OpenAI: say what the text is for

prompt: Marginalia stores Cohere vectors of its help centre to search them for years. Which of these should be stored beside each vector? Choose all that apply.
hint: What would a later query need to know to be made the same way?

choices.text: The model that produced it
choices.why: Yes. Vectors from different models cannot be compared, so a query must be made by the same one.

choices.text: The `input_type` it was embedded with
choices.why: Yes. It decides which type the queries need, and it is invisible in the numbers.

choices.text: The encoding it was stored in, such as `int8`
choices.why: Yes. The encoding decides how every later query has to be scored against it.

choices.text: The tokens the call was billed for
choices.why: That is a fact about the invoice. No later query needs it to be compared correctly.

choices.text: The HTTP status of the request that made it
choices.why: A stored vector came from a successful request by definition, so the status says nothing.

prompt: Order these vectors from the most bytes to the fewest.
hint: Four bytes per float, one per int8, one bit per binary coordinate.
items: A gemini-embedding-001 float vector of 3,072 numbers
trap: The lab-minilm int8 vector, 384 bytes, is not smaller than the binary one: a lab-wordllama ubinary vector is 32 bytes.

prompt: Binary vectors are compared by counting the bit positions where they differ, a measure called the ___ distance.
hint: Named after a mathematician who worked on error-correcting codes.
